name: Mercury skin lightening cream

lead: Mercury-containing lightening creams use inorganic mercury salts to suppress melanin production, which lightens the skin and fades dark patches. People who use them are generally seeking a lighter or more even complexion.

The approach has a long history: bleaching cosmetics containing mercury are reported from ancient Greece and Rome and from 19th-century America. Today the products are illegal in many countries but are still sold informally and online, and health researchers have linked prolonged use to kidney and neurological complications [1].

paras: The creams are applied to the face or body over weeks to months. Mercury is often not listed among the ingredients, so users may not know a product contains it [1]. Visible lightening is the intended result.

Mercury accumulates in the skin and body. Reported harms include skin discoloration, kidney damage, and neurological symptoms such as insomnia, memory loss and irritability; pregnancy complications are also noted [1]. Many countries prohibit mercury in cosmetics, though others still permit it [1].

angle.text: Users apply the cream to lighten skin tone or fade pigmentation. The lightening effect is the reason for use; documented systemic and skin harms are the reason regulators in many countries prohibit it.

lead: Mercury skin lightening cream is a category of skin-bleaching product whose active ingredient is an inorganic mercury compound, such as mercuric chloride or ammoniated mercury. People use these creams to lighten overall skin tone or to fade dark spots, with the aim of a paler or more even complexion [1].

Mercury-based whiteners have a long record. Bleaching cosmetics in ancient Greece and Rome are reported to have used mercury alongside white lead, and toxic lead and mercury preparations were sold in 19th-century America [1]. Skin-lightening product use is widespread today: one summary reports regular use by over a quarter of women in several African countries and around 40 percent in Asia [1].

Health researchers describe mercury accumulating in the dermis and, with prolonged use, discoloring the skin, with kidney and neurological complications also reported [1]. Mercury-containing whiteners are illegal in many countries, but mercury is frequently undeclared, and products can still be bought online [1].

Banned in many countries; permitted in some [1]

paras: These creams contain inorganic mercury compounds as the lightening agent. Such products have been found in skin whiteners from several countries, including creams from Pakistan found to contain toxic mercury levels [1]. Because mercury is often not declared as an ingredient, consumers can be unaware of its presence [1].

Mercury and white lead were reportedly used in bleaching cosmetics in ancient Greece and Rome [1]. In the 19th century, American products with toxic doses of lead and mercury were used, mainly by white women [1]. South Africa banned products containing mercury or high levels of hydroquinone beginning in the 1970s [1].

Mercury compounds can cause neurological and kidney problems, and mercury accumulates in the dermis, where prolonged use can discolor the skin [1]. A study led by Antoine Mahé linked long-term use to renal and neurological complications including insomnia, memory loss and irritability [1]. The World Health Organization has noted inorganic mercury in skin-lightening products and associates it with skin cancer, and pregnant users may face complications [1]. Acute exposure can cause pneumonitis and gastric irritation [1].
Some countries ban mercury compounds in cosmetics while others still permit them [1]. Where banned, products are still reported to circulate, including through online sales [1].

No studies found on the cosmetic effectiveness of mercury creams as a treatment. Published work consists of toxicology reports and case studies of adverse effects, summarized in reviews such as that cited above [1].
